transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Hi Dr. Smith. Well, I came in because I just can't seem to stop worrying about everything at once. It's just constant. I'm worried about my marriage, whether my performance is slipping at work, the bills, all these house projects I keep dropping... Honestly, I just keep worrying that I'm basically failing as a husband and a father. It's just gotten to be too much to handle on my own.
Do you ever experience sudden, intense surges of fear where your heart starts racing or you feel like you might be having a medical emergency?

No, not really. I don't get those sudden spikes of fear where I feel like I'm having a heart attack or anything like that. It's... it's not a sudden emergency feeling. It's just more of a constant, grinding worry that's always there, all day long. My mind just races constantly, but I've never felt like I needed to go to the hospital or anything.
How long have you been feeling this way, and did this period of constant worry begin after a specific event in your life?

Well, it's been going on for about nine months now. It really started when this big cloud migration project ramped up at work. And right around that same time, the arguments at home started becoming a regular thing. So, yeah, I'd say it's been about nine months of feeling like this constantly.
Do you find that you worry about a wide variety of topics beyond just your job and your marriage, such as minor things like routine appointments, chores, or even just what might happen tomorrow?

Um, I'm not really sure about the minor things. I haven't really noticed myself stressing over routine appointments or basic chores, I don't think. It's mostly just tied to the big stuff I mentioned before—work, my marriage, the bills, those house projects I'm behind on. 

I mean, I guess I do worry about tomorrow, but mostly just because I know I have to face all those same heavy things again. But no, I wouldn't really say I'm focused on the minor everyday stuff you're asking about.
Do you feel that the level of distress you are experiencing is disproportionate to the actual severity of the problems you are facing at work and at home?

I'm not really sure how to measure if it's out of proportion. I mean... the problems are very real. If this migration project goes sideways, it's a massive failure for my team. And the issues with my wife are serious. So to me, the worry feels justified. 

But... I don't know, maybe the fact that it's completely draining me and I can't ever seem to turn it off means it's too much. I just know it feels overwhelming all the time. I couldn't really tell you if my reaction is disproportionate to the actual problems, though, because to me, the problems just feel huge.
If those specific stressors—the work project and the issues with your marriage—were to be resolved tomorrow, do you feel like you would be able to stop worrying and return to your normal self?

I... honestly, I don't know. I'd like to think so. I'd like to think that if the project finished up perfectly and my wife and I just... fixed everything, that I'd be fine again. 

But if I'm being completely honest, I'm not sure I would be. It's like... even if those things went away, my brain would just find something else to fill that space. It's been so long since I felt normal, I don't really know if just taking away the current problems would actually turn off the worrying.
Aside from your racing mind, have you been experiencing any physical symptoms like muscle tension, headaches, or feeling restless and unable to sit still?

Yeah, actually. I feel wound tight pretty much all day. It's like my shoulders are just locked up, and I'm constantly bracing for something bad to happen. And the restlessness... yeah, I definitely have that. I catch myself pacing around my office between meetings, and even when I go to my chess club, I'm just tapping the pieces or fidgeting. Sitting still just feels impossible right now.
Have you noticed any change in your ability to enjoy activities that you used to find pleasurable, such as your chess club or other hobbies?

I wouldn't say I've lost the ability to enjoy things entirely. I still go to chess club, and I still like playing. It's just... harder to focus on the game because my mind is always somewhere else. But the actual enjoyment of the game is still there, when I can actually concentrate on it. So, no, I don't think my ability to enjoy my hobbies has really changed, just my ability to be present for them.
